In the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), 3234 subjects with impaired glucose tolerance and 
a mean BMI of 34 kg/m2 were randomly assigned to one of three intervention groups, which 
included intensive lifestyle modification or a medicine treatment group, metformin or placebo. 
After an average follow-up of 2.8 years, the lifestyle group reduced the onset of diabetes by 58 
percent while the metformin group reduced the onset of diabetes by 31 percent compared to 
placebo. The goals of the lifestyle intervention were at least a 7 percent weight reduction and a total 
of 150 minutes per week of physical activity. On average, 50 percent of the lifestyle group achieved 
this weight reduction goal, losing an average of 5.6 kg (∼12 lb) and 74 percent maintained the 
required amount of physical activity.
Results from the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes trial, a long-term follow-up of the 
DPP, demonstrated that the reduction in risk of developing diabetes can be sustained over time. 
Eighty-eight percent of all eligible surviving DPP participants joined the DPPOS. After an average 
follow-up of 10 years, the lifestyle intervention and metformin groups reduced the risk of develop­
ing type 2 diabetes by 34 percent and 18 percent respectively compared to placebo.
